source.title_on_document: Human-AI Collaboration for Brainstorming: Effect of the Presence of AI Ideas on Breadth of Exploration

paper_design_summary: This paper reanalyzes brainstorming data collected for an unnamed previous study that was under review (PDF pp. 1 and 4, Introduction and Section 3.2). In university courses, students were individually randomized to brainstorm ways to reduce food waste with or without access to GPT-3.5 suggestions; 52 people were analyzed after exclusions (PDF pp. 4-5, Sections 3.1 and 4). A condition-blind assistant classified ideas into categories, and the authors compared per-participant category breadth with accepted AI ideas included and with AI-origin ideas excluded, alongside idea-quantity measures (PDF pp. 5-6, Sections 3.3 and 4.1).

studies.label: Food-waste brainstorming with or without GPT-3.5 suggestions (reanalysis)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual participants were assigned to human-only brainstorming or human+AI brainstorming with access to requested GPT-3.5 ideas. Coded field_rct because the experiment was conducted in university courses (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1).
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to conditions and were equally distributed across conditions (human-only: 26, human+ai: 26).
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Section 4, first paragraph; setting and conditions: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), Section 3.1.

arms.name: human-only
arms.description: Each participant brainstormed individually using the app, without AI suggestions; baseline condition. PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), Section 3.1. Analyzed count from PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Section 4.

arms.name: human+AI
arms.description: Each participant brainstormed with a GLM through an app that supplied ideas on request; participants were asked to request suggestions at least once and could copy suggestions into their list of ideas. Only accepted suggestions counted toward their results. PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), Sections 3.1-3.2. Analyzed count from PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Section 4.

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 54 participants and excludes two students because of incomplete data and a misunderstanding of the task, leaving 52 analyzed. The timing of exclusions relative to random assignment and the excluded participants' arms are not stated. The total randomized count is therefore left null. Separately, seven unclassified ideas and all deleted ideas were excluded from idea analyses; these are output exclusions, not additional participant exclusions. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Sections 3.3 and 4.
participants.who: University students enrolled mostly in informatics study programs. The experiment took place in three courses at the authors' university's informatics department: design science research, computer-supported cooperative work, and data-driven solutions for the smart city. PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), Section 3.1; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Section 4.
participants.quote: Our study had 54 participants. We had to exclude the data of two students (due to incomplete data and due to a misunderstanding with regard to the task).
participants.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Section 4, first paragraph. Section 3.3 on the same page describes the participants' university as Western European but does not name the country.

ai_tool.how_used: An on-demand brainstorming app displayed three AI suggestions at a time beside the participant's ideas. Participants could accept/copy suggestions into their own list and add, edit or remove ideas. A fixed prompt template incorporated the brainstorming question, current ideas, and past AI ideas; temperature was 0.9. This was a suggestion-request interface rather than free-form chat. PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), Sections 3.1-3.2 and Figure 2; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), continuation of Section 3.2.

task.description: Generate ideas answering: How can we reduce food waste? Participants then selected their best ideas and completed a post-questionnaire. The category-coverage analyses concern the brainstorming idea lists. PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), Section 3.1; PDF pp. 5-6 (printed pp. 425-426), Section 4.1.
task.duration: 10 minutes of brainstorming; participation took about 30 minutes overall. PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), Section 3.1.

outcomes.name: Flexibility of the final idea set, including accepted AI suggestions (H1)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Distinct categories covered by each participant's final list of ideas, including accepted/copied AI suggestions in the human+AI condition. A student assistant blind to condition classified ideas using the predefined Specht and Buck (2019) system of 13 categories within five clusters. Unclassified and deleted ideas were excluded. The paper calls this team-level flexibility, but calculates one score per participant; a human+AI team contains one human. This is within-participant category breadth, not similarity across people. The 115 accepted AI suggestions enter this outcome; all 373 AI suggestions in Table 2 do not. PDF pp. 4-6 (printed pp. 424-426), Sections 3.1, 3.3 and 4.1, Tables 1-2 and Figure 3.

contrasts.reported: human+AI: mdn=5; human-only: mdn=2; Mann-Whitney U=546.5, p<.001; rank-biserial correlation rB=.617. The paragraph also reports mean=4.115 for category coverage, without labeling it as an arm-specific mean. The reported effect size is a rank-biserial correlation, not a standardized mean difference. No arm SDs, SE or confidence interval are printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), Section 4.1, paragraph continuing from PDF p. 5 and Figure 3.

outcomes.name: Flexibility of human-origin ideas only (H2)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Distinct categories covered by each participant's human-origin ideas, excluding all AI-origin ideas from the human+AI condition. Uses the same condition-blind classification and predefined 13-category system as H1. AI remained available while participants generated the scored human-origin ideas; excluding AI text from scoring does not make this an after-AI outcome. PDF pp. 5-6 (printed pp. 425-426), Sections 3.3 and 4.1, Table 1 and Figure 4.

contrasts.reported: Mann-Whitney U=326.0, p=.830. The paragraph reports mean=2.846 for human-origin category coverage, without labeling it as an arm-specific mean. The authors report no significant difference between conditions; arm-specific numerical summaries and an effect size are not provided in the text.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), Section 4.1, paragraph on the second hypothesis and Figure 4.

outcomes.name: Human within-category fluency
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: For each participant, the average number of human-contributed ideas per category covered; participants with no ideas receive 0. This is the paper's within-category fluency measure, a ratio rather than total idea count. PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), Section 4.1, final paragraph.

contrasts.reported: human-only: mdn=2; human+ai: mdn=1; Mann-Whitney U=119.0, p<.001. No effect size, SE or confidence interval is printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), Section 4.1, final paragraph before Section 4.2.

outcomes.name: Number of human-origin ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of human-origin ideas contributed in each condition. Table 2 supplies condition totals and means; Section 4.1 discusses the condition comparison as a finding from the prior study using these data. The availability tag for arm descriptives refers to the printed means and analyzed people counts; SDs are not given. PDF pp. 5-6 (printed pp. 425-426), Section 4 and Table 2, and Section 4.1.

contrasts.reported: human+AI: 87 human-origin ideas (mean=3.3); human-only: 140 human-origin ideas (mean=5.4); analyzed people: human-only: 26, human+ai: 26. Table 2 reports 227 human-origin ideas in total. No SDs or numerical test for this contrast are printed. Section 4.1 states that human-only participants contributed significantly more ideas, referring to the previous study; Section 5.1 later states that no significant difference in human idea number was observed. The conflicting significance descriptions are unresolved; direction here follows the printed descriptive means.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Section 4, participant paragraph and Table 2; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), Section 4.1; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 428), Section 5.1.

outcomes.name: Joint human-and-AI idea quantity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The discussion reports joint idea quantity for the human+AI condition versus the human-only condition. No numerical contrast or complete definition of this quantity analysis is printed. Section 3.1 says only ideas in the participant's list count toward results, and Section 4.1 identifies the accepted AI subset. Table 2 includes all analyzed AI suggestions and therefore cannot be read as the final accepted joint output count. Retained because it is an output-based quantity result explicitly reported by the paper. PDF pp. 4-7 (printed pp. 424-427), Sections 3.1, 4, 4.1 and 5.1.

contrasts.reported: Section 5.1 states that the human working with the AI jointly produced significantly more ideas than alone. No numerical effect, arm means for accepted joint output, test statistic or p-value accompanies this claim. Table 2's human+AI total of 460 includes 373 AI suggestions and 87 human ideas; Section 4.1 says 115 AI suggestions were accepted/copied. No final joint count or effect has been calculated here.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), Section 5.1, final paragraph; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Table 2; PDF pp. 5-6 (printed pp. 425-426), Section 4.1.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: An unnamed previous study, under review at the time, analyzing the quantity, novelty and value of individual ideas from the same data. The present paper explicitly states that it reuses those data. The original paper's title, full citation and eventual publication are not identified here.
sample_overlap.quote: We collected the data for a different study (under review) with a focus on understanding how AI suggestions affect idea quantity and quality.
sample_overlap.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), Section 3.2; PDF p. 1 (printed p. 421), Introduction; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), Section 4.1.

company_involvement.description: No company authorship or commercial funding is stated. Both authors are affiliated with Universität Hamburg, and the acknowledgment names funding by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research for project HyMeKI. OpenAI is identified as the model provider, not as a research funder or collaborator.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 421), author affiliations; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), Section 3.2; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 429), Acknowledgment.

eligibility.reason: Participants were randomly assigned to human-only versus human+AI brainstorming (PDF p. 5, printed p. 425, Section 4); the latter had access to generative AI while producing their ideas (PDF p. 4, printed p. 424, Sections 3.1-3.2). The analyzed sample was 52 people, with 26 in each arm, after two participant exclusions (PDF p. 5, Section 4), meeting the threshold. Distinct idea categories were scored from produced output by a condition-blind coder and compared per participant (PDF pp. 5-6, printed pp. 425-426, Sections 3.3 and 4.1, Figures 3-4). This is a reanalysis of a randomized human-assistance experiment; its original sample must be linked before pooling.

one_line_finding: Among 52 analyzed students, final idea sets including accepted AI suggestions covered a median of 5 categories versus 2 without AI (U=546.5, p<.001, rB=.617), while human-origin category coverage showed no significant difference (U=326.0, p=.830; PDF p. 5, Section 4, and p. 6, Section 4.1, Figures 3-4).
open_questions: Which publication is the unnamed previous study under review whose data are reused? The PDF establishes overlap but supplies no title or full citation (PDF pp. 1 and 4, Introduction and Section 3.2).

What were the total and per-arm counts at random assignment, and when were the participant exclusions applied? Only overall participation and post-exclusion arm counts are identified (PDF p. 5, Section 4).

Can the conflicting statements about the significance of the human-origin idea-count comparison be resolved? Section 4.1 calls it significant (PDF p. 6), whereas Section 5.1 describes no significant difference (PDF p. 8); no numerical test is printed for this comparison.

What exact accepted-output definition and statistics support the joint idea-quantity claim in Section 5.1 (PDF p. 7)? Table 2 includes unaccepted AI suggestions and cannot substitute for the final output analysis (PDF pp. 5-6).
notes: The entire markdown was read through the references; it contains no appendix. The PDF has no stated supplement, preregistration, or data/code repository link. All recorded results and counts were checked against the corresponding PDF text. Locators distinguish PDF page numbers from the printed proceedings page numbers. The single dataset remains one study despite the additional analyses by idea origin. PDF p. 5, Table 2 reports 600 analyzed ideas (373 AI-origin and 227 human-origin); these are not participant counts. Section 4.1 uses 115 accepted AI suggestions for final-list flexibility (PDF pp. 5-6). The primary category-coverage outcomes are flexibility within each participant's list, despite the paper's use of the word diversity, and are not across_people estimates. Section 4.2 additionally compares pooled category profiles of AI-origin and human-origin ideas (13 versus 12 categories; PDF p. 6, continuing onto p. 7 and Figure 5), and reports new-category contributions in 41.2% of AI cases versus 41.9% of human cases within the human+AI condition (PDF p. 7). These origin and process descriptions do not compare diversity across people by assistance condition and are not separate eligible outcome contrasts. Open-ended perceptions in Section 4.3 (PDF p. 7) are not scored-output outcomes. Novelty and value are described as the focus of the prior study (PDF p. 1), with no such outcome statistics reported here. The quantity/category-breadth association is reported as Spearman’s ρ=.817, p<.001 (PDF p. 6, Section 4.1), and is not an AI-assistance effect. No effect sizes or final-output totals were computed.
